title: The Autonomous Computer: Infrastructure for Computer Use Agents — Ang Li, Simular
talk_summary: Ang Li of Simular describes building computer-use agents as a neurosymbolic system: a probabilistic VLM agent for exploration plus a deterministic code layer (Simulan) that records successful trajectories and replays them, falling back to the VLM only when the environment changes. He also reports that agents degrade ~10% when run repeatedly (pass^k), and that forcing clarification questions improves reliability.

takeaways.technique: Compile successful agent runs into replayable code/skills
takeaways.what_they_do: The VLM agent writes its successful trajectory as code to a file; next run executes that code first (no LLM calls) and only falls back to the neural agent when the code breaks, with a healing loop that rewrites it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the second time you run the workflow maybe 50% of the effort is done by code without any LM request
takeaways.numbers: claims ~50% of effort done by code on repeat runs; token consumption target 'eventually become zero'

takeaways.technique: Measure pass^k (repeat-run reliability), not just pass@k
takeaways.what_they_do: They ran the best OSWorld agents 3x and measured pass^3, finding success drops ~10% versus single-run scores, worse under perturbed environments; they argue no benchmark captures this.
takeaways.evidence_quote: all the agents has degraded performance in there they almost dropped 10% success rate
takeaways.numbers: ~10% success-rate drop from pass@1 to pass^3

takeaways.what_they_do: They add a prompt instructing the agent to ask clarifying questions on ambiguous parts of the instruction while minimizing unnecessary questions, which raised repeat-run reliability across models.
takeaways.evidence_quote: ask the agent to to ask you clarification clarification questions when you give them the instruction
takeaways.numbers: reported reliability improvement across Claude and GPT-5-based agents (no hard number in transcript)

takeaways.what_they_do: After filling a form, they reverse it and ask the model whether the result makes sense; verification is easier than generation, and failures are fed back for another attempt.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you take a form reverse it and ask the model does that make sense ... verification is is much easier than generation

takeaways.technique: Multi-agent test-time scaling with a small specialist model
takeaways.what_they_do: Their harness runs manager/worker layers and combines a large model with a fine-tuned 7B open-source model specialized for screen grounding; multiple workers attacking the same task improved success at fixed total budget.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you have two foundation models within the same harness it's better than one
takeaways.numbers: 10 agents scaled better than fewer at equal total resource budget; 7B second model gave ~20% gain over big-lab agents (their claim)

takeaways.technique: Code-first guardrails with agent fallback and human approval
takeaways.what_they_do: Irreversible actions are caught by a deterministic rule layer that halts and requests approval; only unmatched cases escalate to the agent, then to a human.
takeaways.evidence_quote: whenever there's a action that recognize that irreversible action the guaro will say stop there
